items.elicits: For each of Document 1 and Document 2, states the author, the year, and the audience the author was most likely trying to reach, one line each.

claims.supports: This evidence can only confirm that a compliant sourcing response -- author, year, and audience for each document -- was returned; it cannot confirm that H1 describes what the student personally can do.
does_not_support: Whether the student, rather than an AI assistant or a quick internet search, produced the author/year/audience answers -- authorship is indistinguishable under these conditions.
Whether the student can source an unfamiliar document under any time constraint, since time is not stated and any resource, including AI, is permitted.
This is easily mistaken for evidence of H3 (explaining authorial motive), but H1 only requires factual identification, not an explanation of why the author wrote as they did.
Whether the audience answer reflects reading-based inference from the document's own language versus a fact looked up about the publication.

delegation.reason: AI is permitted and the work is unsupervised, so a model or a quick search can return the author, year, and audience for a named, published document without the student reading it.

claims.gap_statement: We cannot tell from this assessment whether the student, rather than an outside resource, identified each document's author, year, and audience.

items.elicits: States, in one sentence each, how Document 1 and Document 2 explain the same fact (the rich-poor gap) differently.
Chooses one word or phrase from each document that shows the author's attitude toward great fortunes, and explains what the word choice reveals.

claims.supports: This evidence can only confirm that a compliant response -- a causal contrast between the two documents and a word-choice explanation for each -- was returned; it cannot confirm that H2 describes what the student personally can do.
does_not_support: Whether the student, rather than an AI assistant, produced the causal contrast and the word-choice explanation -- authorship is indistinguishable under these conditions.
Whether the student can identify an attitude-revealing word choice unprompted, since item 3 already directs attention to word choice as the thing to look for.
This is easily mistaken for evidence of H4's point-of-view weighting, but H2 only asks the student to state and contrast the two accounts, not to weigh one against the other in an argument.
Whether the causal contrast reflects the student's own reading versus a second-hand summary of the documents' arguments that an outside tool could generate without the primary text.

delegation.reason: AI is permitted and the work is unsupervised, so a model given the two excerpts can generate both the causal contrast and the word-choice explanation directly.

claims.gap_statement: We cannot tell from this assessment whether the student, rather than an outside resource, contrasted the two authors' causal explanations and read the word choice for attitude.

This is easily mistaken for evidence of H4's point-of-view weighting, but H3 only asks for a motive explanation, not for using that motive to weigh evidence within an argument.

delegation.reason: AI is permitted and the work is unsupervised, so a model can generate a plausible motive explanation for each author from their well-documented historical position without the student reasoning about it.

claims.gap_statement: We cannot tell from this assessment whether the student, rather than an outside resource, explained why each author would write as they did given their position.

items.elicits: Constructs a two-paragraph argument that takes a position addressing both documents, cites evidence from each, explicitly weighs that evidence by each author's point of view, and connects one outside development from the period.

claims.supports: This evidence can only confirm that a compliant two-paragraph argument meeting the rubric's five content elements was returned; it cannot confirm that H4 describes what the student personally can do.
does_not_support: Whether the student, rather than an AI assistant, constructed the argument, selected the evidence, and made the point-of-view weighting explicit -- an unsupervised, AI-permitted take-home cannot distinguish a student's writing from an AI-drafted or AI-revised response.
Whether the student can do this under any time constraint, since time is not stated and resources, including AI, are unconstrained.
Whether the outside-development connection reflects the student's own recalled knowledge versus a fact looked up for the occasion.
The rubric's organization-and-clarity point is not evidence of the reasoning skill itself and can be produced or polished by an outside tool regardless of whether the ideas are the student's own.

delegation.reason: AI is permitted and the work is unsupervised, so a model can draft the entire two-paragraph argument, including evidence selection, point-of-view weighting language, and the outside-development connection.

claims.gap_statement: We cannot tell from this assessment whether the student, rather than an outside resource, constructed the argument, weighed the evidence by point of view, and made the outside-development connection.

gate1_components.carried_forward: Independent production: the argument is visibly the student's own work, not an outside resource's
gate1_components.why: All four named content components of H4 are directly required and scored by item 5's rubric. The one genuinely absent, material component is independent production -- the response cannot be attributed to the student under unsupervised, AI-permitted conditions, and nothing elsewhere in the packet supplies that.

gate2_materiality.why: The purpose is summative and individual, and H4 is the assessment's central claim; without independent production the teacher cannot conclude this student can construct and weigh this kind of argument, only that a compliant-looking essay was returned.

gate3_value.why: Independent evidence for H4 would clearly matter to the summative conclusion -- it is the assessment's central claim -- so pursuing it is worth it in principle, even though (see no_short_check_reason) no short version of the check exists.

claims.no_short_check_reason: H4 asks for a sustained, two-paragraph argument that integrates both documents, weighs them by point of view, and connects an outside development -- each move depends on the others for its meaning, so no few-minute item can require the whole chain without either pre-selecting the evidence or the weighting for the student (removing the judgment being assessed) or ceasing to be short. The only way to get an independent observation of H4 itself is to have the student write this same kind of argument under supervision, which is a different administration of the task, not a small addition to this one.

conditions_echo: Unsupervised, individual, AI-permitted take-home summative assessment, sent home over a week at the end of the industrialization unit; the two documents are new to the students, but sourcing practice has been done on other documents.
reviewer_notes: H1-H3 share one defect: the items ask for the right moves, but unsupervised, AI-permitted take-home conditions mean no response can be attributed to the student, and a short (3-5 minute) supervised check recovers each at low cost. H4 is different in kind -- it is a sustained, integrated argument, and no short check can reach it without pre-digesting the very judgment being assessed. Recovering independent evidence for H4 requires administering this same kind of writing task under supervision; that is a conditions decision for the teacher to make about the assessment as a whole, not a two-minute addition to this one.
